name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q01 - Melvin Calvin carbon assimilation pathway discovery

questiontext.text: Melvin Calvin, along with J.A. Bassham, mapped the pathway of carbon assimilation in photosynthesis by labelling carbon dioxide with which radioactive isotope?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Radioactive tracers allow biochemists to follow the fate of specific atoms through metabolic pathways in living organisms.

Step 2: Evaluation
Melvin Calvin and J.A. Bassham studied reactions in green plants forming sugar and other substances from carbon dioxide, water, and minerals by labelling \(\text{CO}_2\) with radioactive carbon-14 (\(\text{C}^{14}\)). This work earned Calvin the Nobel Prize in 1961.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The radioactive isotope used by Melvin Calvin and J.A. Bassham to label carbon dioxide was \(\text{C}^{14}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q02 - Short distance versus long distance transport

questiontext.text: Over small distances within a flowering plant, substances move by diffusion and by cytoplasmic streaming supplemented by active transport. Transport over longer distances through the vascular system is known as:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Plants lack a circulatory system and rely on specialised vascular tissues (xylem and phloem) to move substances across long distances.

Step 2: Evaluation
While diffusion and cytoplasmic streaming supplemented by active transport handle short-distance movement within cells and tissues, long-distance bulk transport through the xylem and phloem is specifically termed translocation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Long-distance transport through the vascular system is called translocation.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q03 - Direction of transport in flowering plants

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements regarding the direction of transport in rooted flowering plants is incorrect?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Different substances in flowering plants follow distinct directional routes depending on the conducting tissue and physiological need.

Step 2: Evaluation
In rooted plants, transport of water and minerals in the xylem is essentially unidirectional, from roots to stems. Organic and mineral nutrients undergo multidirectional transport: photosynthates are exported from leaves to all parts including storage organs and later re-exported, and mineral nutrients are withdrawn from senescing parts to growing regions. Hormones are transported in very small amounts, sometimes in a strictly polarised or unidirectional manner—never exclusively multidirectional in all cases as claimed by the false statement.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the incorrect statement is that hormones or plant growth regulators are always transported in a multidirectional manner.

answer.text: Transport of water and minerals in xylem is essentially unidirectional, from roots to stems.
Organic nutrients synthesised in leaves are exported to all parts and later re-exported from storage organs.
Hormones or plant growth regulators are always transported in a multidirectional manner from their site of synthesis.
When any plant part undergoes senescence, nutrients may be withdrawn from such regions and moved to growing parts.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q04 - Levels of organisation in biology

questiontext.text: Describing biological structure and variation at the organismic and above level of organisation resulted in ecology, whereas describing them at the cellular and molecular level resulted in:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Biology encompasses two major perspectives resting on different levels of organisation of life forms and phenomena.

Step 2: Evaluation
The perspective focused on organismic and higher levels of organisation led to ecology and related disciplines, whereas the perspective focused on cellular and molecular levels led to physiology and biochemistry.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The cellular and molecular level perspective resulted in physiology and biochemistry.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q05 - Diffusion as only means for gaseous movement

questiontext.text: Which process is the only means for gaseous movement within the plant body?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Gases such as oxygen and carbon dioxide move across intercellular spaces and membranes in plants down their partial pressure or concentration gradients.

Step 2: Evaluation
Diffusion is a passive, slow process that does not depend on a living system. It is the sole mechanism for gaseous movement within the plant body.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Diffusion is the only means for gaseous movement within the plant body.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q06 - Factors affecting rate of simple diffusion

questiontext.text: Which of the following sets of factors affects the rate of simple diffusion across a membrane?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Simple diffusion is driven by random molecular motion down a concentration gradient and is influenced by physical conditions and membrane properties.

Step 2: Evaluation
Diffusion rates are affected by the concentration gradient, permeability of the separating membrane, temperature, and pressure. ATP supply and protein side-chain inhibitors do not affect simple diffusion.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Concentration gradient, membrane permeability, temperature, and pressure are the factors affecting diffusion rate.

answer.text: ATP concentration, temperature, and carrier protein saturation
Concentration gradient, membrane permeability, temperature, and pressure
Protein side-chain inhibitors, pH, and ATP hydrolysis
Hormonal regulation, concentration gradient, and ATP supply

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q07 - Diffusion in solids versus diffusion of solids

questiontext.text: With respect to the physical states of matter, which statement about diffusion is accurate?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Diffusion depends on the freedom of random molecular motion in a medium.

Step 2: Evaluation
Diffusion is obvious in gases and liquids because their molecules move freely. In the case of solids, diffusion in solids (such as gases or liquids diffusing through a solid matrix) is more likely than diffusion of solids themselves.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Diffusion is obvious in gases and liquids, and diffusion in solids is more likely rather than of solids.

answer.text: Diffusion of solids is faster than diffusion in liquids.
Diffusion of solids is more likely than diffusion in solids.
Diffusion is obvious in gases and liquids, and diffusion in solids is more likely rather than of solids.
Diffusion occurs only in gases and never in liquids or solids.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q08 - Characteristics of facilitated diffusion

questiontext.text: Which of the following is not a characteristic of facilitated diffusion?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Facilitated diffusion uses special membrane proteins to move hydrophilic substances across a lipid bilayer without metabolic energy.

Step 2: Evaluation
Facilitated diffusion is highly specific, shows saturation when all protein transporters are occupied, and is sensitive to inhibitors that react with protein side chains. However, it cannot set up a concentration gradient or cause net transport from a low to a high concentration—a gradient must already be present.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Causing net transport of molecules from a low to a high concentration is a property of active transport, not facilitated diffusion.

answer.text: It reaches a maximum rate when all protein transporters are being used.
It is sensitive to inhibitors that react with protein side chains.
It allows the cell to select specific substances for uptake.
It causes net transport of molecules from a lower to a higher concentration.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q09 - Porins in outer membranes of organelles and bacteria

questiontext.text: Porins are proteins that form large pores allowing molecules up to the size of small proteins to pass through the outer membranes of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Certain membrane channel proteins form large, non-specific pores in outer membranes of endosymbiotic organelles and prokaryotes.

Step 2: Evaluation
Porins are found in the outer membranes of plastids, mitochondria, and some bacteria, where they allow molecules up to the size of small proteins to cross.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Porins form large pores in the outer membranes of plastids, mitochondria, and some bacteria.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q10 - Aquaporins forming water channels

questiontext.text: Water channels that facilitate the movement of water across biological membranes are made up of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Water movement across membranes is facilitated by specialised protein channels.

Step 2: Evaluation
Water channels in biological membranes are composed of eight different types of aquaporins.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Water channels are made up of eight different types of aquaporins.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q11 - Passive symport antiport and uniport

questiontext.text: When a carrier protein allows facilitated diffusion only if two types of molecules cross the membrane simultaneously in opposite directions, the transport is termed:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Carrier proteins in facilitated diffusion are classified based on whether one or two molecule types are transported and their relative directions.

Step 2: Evaluation
In a symport, both molecules cross in the same direction. In an antiport, two molecules cross in opposite directions. In a uniport, a single molecule moves independently of other molecules.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Simultaneous movement of two types of molecules in opposite directions is called antiport.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q12 - Shared properties of facilitated and active transport

questiontext.text: Which property is shared by both facilitated diffusion and active transport, but is absent in simple diffusion?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Both facilitated diffusion and active transport are mediated by specific membrane proteins, whereas simple diffusion occurs directly across the membrane without carrier proteins.

Step 2: Evaluation
Because both facilitated diffusion and active transport rely on membrane proteins, they share the properties of being highly selective, reaching transport saturation, responding to protein inhibitors, and being under hormonal regulation. Only active transport requires ATP energy and performs uphill transport.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Transport saturation and high selectivity are shared by facilitated diffusion and active transport, but absent in simple diffusion.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q13 - Water content in watermelon and herbaceous plants

questiontext.text: Most herbaceous plants have only about what percentage of their fresh weight as dry matter?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Water constitutes the bulk of the fresh weight in soft, herbaceous plant tissues.

Step 2: Evaluation
While a watermelon has over 92 per cent water, most herbaceous plants have about 85 to 90 per cent water and only about 10 to 15 per cent of their fresh weight as dry matter.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Most herbaceous plants have about 10 to 15 per cent of their fresh weight as dry matter.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q14 - Daily water absorption in corn and mustard plants

questiontext.text: A mature corn plant absorbs almost three litres of water in a day, whereas a mustard plant absorbs water equal to its own weight in about:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Terrestrial plants absorb large volumes of water daily because most of it is lost through transpiration.

Step 2: Evaluation
A mature corn plant absorbs nearly three litres of water per day, while a mustard plant absorbs water equal to its own weight in approximately 5 hours.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A mustard plant absorbs water equal to its own weight in about 5 hours.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q15 - Water potential of pure water and units

questiontext.text: By convention, the water potential (\(\Psi_w\)) of pure water at standard temperatures, which is not under any pressure, is taken to be:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Water potential is a measure of the free energy of water molecules, expressed in pressure units such as pascals (\(\text{Pa}\)).

Step 2: Evaluation
Pure water has the greatest concentration of water molecules and thus the maximum water potential. By convention, at standard temperatures and atmospheric pressure (not under any extra pressure), its water potential is taken as zero.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The water potential of pure water under standard conditions is zero.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q16 - Water potential of a solution at atmospheric pressure

questiontext.text: For a solution kept open at atmospheric pressure, what is the relationship between its water potential (\(\Psi_w\)) and solute potential (\(\Psi_s\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The water potential of a system is the sum of its solute potential and pressure potential: \(\Psi_w = \Psi_s + \Psi_p\).

Step 2: Evaluation
For an open solution at atmospheric pressure, no extra hydrostatic pressure is applied, so \(\Psi_p = 0\). Substituting this into the water potential equation yields \(\Psi_w = \Psi_s\), which is always negative.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
At atmospheric pressure, \(\Psi_w = \Psi_s\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q17 - Calculation of water potential and osmotic flow

questiontext.text: Cell X has \(\Psi_s = -15\text{ bars}\) and \(\Psi_p = +5\text{ bars}\). Adjacent cell Y has \(\Psi_s = -20\text{ bars}\) and \(\Psi_p = +12\text{ bars}\). What will be the net direction of water movement between these two cells?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
- For cell X: \(\Psi_s(X) = -15\text{ bars}\), \(\Psi_p(X) = +5\text{ bars}\).
- For cell Y: \(\Psi_s(Y) = -20\text{ bars}\), \(\Psi_p(Y) = +12\text{ bars}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Solute potential is negative, pressure potential is positive in turgid cells, and water moves from a region of higher (less negative) water potential to a region of lower (more negative) water potential.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[\Psi_w = \Psi_s + \Psi_p\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Water potential of cell X:
\[\Psi_w(X) = -15 + 5 = -10\text{ bars}\]
2. Water potential of cell Y:
\[\Psi_w(Y) = -20 + 12 = -8\text{ bars}\]
3. Compare \(\Psi_w(Y)\) and \(\Psi_w(X)\):
Since \(-8\text{ bars} > -10\text{ bars}\), cell Y has a higher water potential than cell X.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Water flows down the water potential gradient from higher (\(-8\text{ bars}\)) to lower (\(-10\text{ bars}\)). Therefore, water moves from cell Y to cell X.

answer.text: No net movement as both are in equilibrium
First from X to Y, then back from Y to X

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q18 - Negative pressure potential in xylem

questiontext.text: Although pressure potential (\(\Psi_p\)) is usually positive in turgid plant cells, where does a negative pressure potential (tension) play a major role in plants?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Pressure potential can be positive (turgor) or negative (tension/suction).

Step 2: Evaluation
In the xylem water column, transpiration from leaves creates a negative pressure potential or tension, which plays a major role in pulling water up a stem.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Negative pressure potential plays a major role in the water column of the xylem for upward water transport.

answer.text: In the central vacuole of guard cells during stomatal opening
In the water column in the xylem for water transport up a stem
In phloem sieve tubes at the source during sucrose loading
In root hairs during imbibition by dry seeds

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q19 - Tonoplast and cell membrane in osmosis

questiontext.text: In plant cells, which two membranes together act as the important determinants of the movement of molecules into or out of the cell?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The cell wall of a plant cell is freely permeable to water and dissolved substances and is not a barrier to movement.

Step 2: Evaluation
In plant cells, the cell membrane (plasma membrane) and the membrane of the large central vacuole (the tonoplast) together regulate the movement of molecules into or out of the cell.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The cell membrane and the tonoplast together determine molecular movement in or out of plant cells.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q20 - Direction of osmosis between positive water potentials

questiontext.text: Two solutions with water potentials \(\Psi_w = 0.2\text{ MPa}\) and \(\Psi_w = 0.1\text{ MPa}\) are separated by a selectively permeable membrane. What will be the direction of net water movement?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Solution 1 has \(\Psi_w = 0.2\text{ MPa}\), and Solution 2 has \(\Psi_w = 0.1\text{ MPa}\), separated by a selectively permeable membrane.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Water always moves spontaneously by osmosis from a region of higher water potential to a region of lower water potential until equilibrium is reached.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Net osmosis direction: Higher \(\Psi_w \rightarrow\) Lower \(\Psi_w\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Compare the two values: \(0.2\text{ MPa} > 0.1\text{ MPa}\). Thus, the solution at \(0.2\text{ MPa}\) has the higher chemical/water potential.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Water will move from the solution with \(\Psi_w = 0.2\text{ MPa}\) to the solution with \(\Psi_w = 0.1\text{ MPa}\).

answer.text: No movement occurs because both values are positive
Solute moves from \(0.1\text{ MPa}\) to \(0.2\text{ MPa}\) instead of water

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q21 - Osmotic pressure versus osmotic potential

questiontext.text: How are osmotic pressure and osmotic (solute) potential related to each other?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Osmotic pressure is the external pressure needed to stop osmotic entry of water into a solution, whereas osmotic potential is the lowering of water potential due to solute particles.

Step 2: Evaluation
Numerically, osmotic pressure is equivalent to osmotic potential, but their signs are opposite: osmotic pressure is the positive pressure applied, while osmotic potential is negative.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Osmotic pressure and osmotic potential are numerically equal but opposite in sign.

answer.text: They are numerically equivalent, but opposite in sign.
Both are always negative and numerically equal.
Osmotic pressure is always twice the osmotic potential.
Both are always positive and independent of solute concentration.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q22 - Thistle funnel osmosis experiment with sucrose

questiontext.text: In the thistle funnel demonstration of osmosis, a sucrose solution in the funnel is separated from pure water in a beaker by a selectively permeable membrane. If the membrane were permeable to sucrose so that sucrose diffused out into the beaker, what would happen?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Osmosis requires a selectively permeable membrane that allows solvent (water) to pass while restricting solute (sucrose) movement, maintaining a solute concentration difference.

Step 2: Evaluation
If sucrose diffuses out through the membrane into the beaker, the solute concentration will eventually equalise on both sides, eliminating the osmotic gradient; the sustained osmotic rise in the funnel would not be maintained at the expected equilibrium level, and the solute would equilibrate across both compartments.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
If sucrose diffused out through the membrane, the concentration gradient would dissipate and the osmotic level rise would not be sustained at equilibrium.

answer.text: The solution level in the funnel would rise indefinitely without stopping.
The osmotic gradient would dissipate as sucrose equilibrates, preventing a sustained osmotic rise.
Water would immediately stop entering the funnel even at time zero.
Pure water in the beaker would turn hypertonic relative to the funnel.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q23 - Space between cell wall and protoplast in plasmolysis

questiontext.text: In a plasmolysed plant cell, what occupies the space between the rigid cell wall and the shrunken protoplast, and what is the pressure potential (\(\Psi_p\)) of a flaccid cell?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The plant cell wall is freely permeable to water and dissolved solutes, whereas the plasma membrane is selectively permeable.

Step 2: Evaluation
When a cell is placed in a hypertonic solution, the protoplast shrinks away from the cell wall. Because the cell wall is freely permeable, the external hypertonic solution passes through the cell wall and occupies the space between the wall and the shrunken protoplast. In a flaccid cell (at equilibrium in an isotonic solution), there is no turgor pressure built up against the wall, so \(\Psi_p = 0\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The hypertonic external solution occupies the space between the cell wall and shrunken protoplast, and \(\Psi_p\) of a flaccid cell is zero.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q24 - Prerequisites for imbibition

questiontext.text: Which two conditions are essential prerequisites for any solid substance to imbibe a liquid?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Imbibition is a special type of diffusion where water is absorbed by solid colloids, causing them to increase in volume.

Step 2: Evaluation
For imbibition to occur, there must be (1) a water potential gradient between the absorbent and the liquid imbibed, and (2) an affinity between the adsorbent and the liquid.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A water potential gradient and affinity between the adsorbent and the liquid are essential for imbibition.

answer.text: ATP hydrolysis and a selectively permeable membrane
Positive turgor pressure and suberised cell walls
Water potential gradient and affinity between the adsorbent and the liquid

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q25 - Characteristics of mass or bulk flow

questiontext.text: How does mass (bulk) flow differ from simple diffusion in plants?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Long-distance translocation in plants occurs via mass or bulk flow rather than diffusion alone.

Step 2: Evaluation
Mass flow is the movement of substances in bulk from one point to another due to pressure differences (either positive or negative hydrostatic pressure gradients). Substances, whether in solution or suspension, are swept along at the same pace as in a flowing river, unlike diffusion where different substances move independently down their individual concentration gradients.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
In mass flow, substances in solution or suspension move together at the same pace due to a pressure difference.

answer.text: Substances in solution or suspension are swept along at the same pace due to pressure differences.
Different solutes move independently according to their individual concentration gradients.
Mass flow can only occur through a positive hydrostatic pressure gradient and never by suction.
Mass flow is slower than diffusion over long distances.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q26 - Structure and absorption by root hairs

questiontext.text: Root hairs, which greatly increase the surface area for absorption of water and mineral solutes, are thin-walled slender extensions of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Plants absorb most of their water and minerals through millions of root hairs located near the root tips.

Step 2: Evaluation
Root hairs are thin-walled slender extensions of root epidermal cells that absorb water along with mineral solutes purely by diffusion.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Root hairs are extensions of root epidermal cells.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q27 - Apoplast pathway of water movement

questiontext.text: Which of the following is true regarding the apoplastic movement of water in plant roots?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The apoplast is the continuous system of adjacent cell walls throughout the plant, interrupted only at the Casparian strips of the root endodermis.

Step 2: Evaluation
Apoplastic movement occurs exclusively through intercellular spaces and cell walls, does not involve crossing any cell membrane, and proceeds via mass flow driven by tension and the adhesive and cohesive properties of water.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Apoplastic movement occurs through intercellular spaces and cell walls without crossing the cell membrane.

answer.text: It involves crossing the plasma membrane of every cortical cell.
It is aided by cytoplasmic streaming through plasmodesmata.
It occurs through intercellular spaces and cell walls without crossing the cell membrane.
It is completely blocked in the cortex because cortical cells are tightly packed.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q28 - Symplastic movement and cytoplasmic streaming

questiontext.text: During symplastic movement of water, intercellular movement between neighbouring cells occurs through \(\underline{\hspace{2cm}}\), and may be aided by cytoplasmic streaming as easily observed in \(\underline{\hspace{2cm}}\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The symplastic system consists of interconnected protoplasts.

Step 2: Evaluation
Neighbouring cells are connected by cytoplasmic strands extending through plasmodesmata. Symplastic movement is relatively slower because water enters cells across the cell membrane, and it may be aided by cytoplasmic streaming, which is easily visible as chloroplast movement in cells of the Hydrilla leaf.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pair is plasmodesmata and Hydrilla leaf.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q29 - Symplastic transition at endodermis and xylem apoplast

questiontext.text: Once water enters the xylem vessels and tracheids in young roots, these conduits are considered parts of which pathway?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Water movement through the root layers is forced into the symplast at the endodermis due to the suberised Casparian strip.

Step 2: Evaluation
After crossing the endodermis symplastically and passing through a membrane to reach the xylem, water enters the xylem vessels and/or tracheids. Because xylem vessels and tracheids are non-living conduits without protoplasts, they are parts of the apoplast.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Xylem vessels and tracheids are non-living conduits and are therefore parts of the apoplast.

answer.text: Symplast, because they are lined by Casparian strips

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q30 - Obligate mycorrhizal association in Pinus

questiontext.text: In a mycorrhizal association, what do the plant roots provide to the symbiotic fungus?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Mycorrhiza is a mutually beneficial symbiotic association between a fungus and a plant root system.

Step 2: Evaluation
The fungal hyphae absorb mineral ions and water from a large volume of soil and provide them to the roots; in return, the roots provide sugars and nitrogen-containing compounds to the mycorrhizae.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The plant roots provide sugars and N-containing compounds to the fungus.

answer.text: Mineral ions and water from the soil

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q31 - Root pressure and guttation

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements about root pressure is incorrect?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Root pressure is a positive pressure generated inside the xylem when ions are actively transported into root vascular tissues and water follows osmotically.

Step 2: Evaluation
Root pressure can push water to small heights, causes guttation at night or early morning when evaporation is low, and re-establishes continuous water chains in the xylem that break under transpiration tension. However, it provides only a modest push and does not account for the majority of water transport in tall trees (which is driven by transpiration pull).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Stating that root pressure accounts for the majority of water transport in tall trees is incorrect.

answer.text: It is a positive pressure built up inside the xylem due to active ion transport into root vascular tissues.
Its effect is observable as guttation at night and early morning when evaporation is low.
It accounts for the majority of water transport up to the top of tall trees.
Its greatest contribution is re-establishing continuous chains of water molecules in the xylem.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q32 - Rate of xylem flow and water utilisation in leaves

questiontext.text: Upward flow of water through the xylem can achieve rates up to \(15\text{ metres per hour}\). Approximately what fraction of the water reaching the leaves is actually used in photosynthesis and plant growth?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Water is transient in plants; almost all water absorbed and transported to the leaves is lost to the atmosphere.

Step 2: Evaluation
Less than 1 per cent of the water reaching the leaves is used in photosynthesis and plant growth, while most of it is lost through stomata by transpiration.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Less than 1 per cent of the water reaching the leaves is used in photosynthesis and plant growth.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q33 - Guard cell microfibril orientation and stomatal opening

questiontext.text: How are cellulose microfibrils oriented in the cell walls of guard cells to make the opening of the stoma easier?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The immediate cause of stomatal opening and closing is a change in the turgidity of guard cells, assisted by their wall architecture.

Step 2: Evaluation
Cellulose microfibrils in the cell walls of guard cells are oriented radially rather than longitudinally, which makes it easier for the stoma to open when turgidity increases.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Cellulose microfibrils in guard cell walls are oriented radially.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q34 - Stomatal distribution in dorsiventral and isobilateral leaves

questiontext.text: Which statement accurately describes the distribution of stomata on dorsiventral and isobilateral leaves?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Stomatal distribution differs between dicotyledonous (dorsiventral) and monocotyledonous (isobilateral) leaves.

Step 2: Evaluation
Usually, the lower surface of a dorsiventral (often dicotyledonous) leaf has a greater number of stomata, whereas in an isobilateral (often monocotyledonous) leaf, stomata are about equal on both surfaces.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A dorsiventral leaf has more stomata on the lower surface, while an isobilateral leaf has approximately equal numbers on both surfaces.

answer.text: A dorsiventral leaf has equal stomata on both surfaces, while an isobilateral leaf has more on the upper surface.
A dorsiventral leaf has more stomata on the lower surface, while an isobilateral leaf has about equal numbers on both surfaces.
Both dorsiventral and isobilateral leaves have stomata exclusively on the lower surface.
A dorsiventral leaf has more stomata on the upper surface, while an isobilateral leaf has none on the upper surface.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q35 - External and plant factors affecting transpiration

questiontext.text: Which of the following is classified as a plant factor rather than an external factor affecting transpiration?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Transpiration is regulated by both environmental (external) factors and internal/anatomical (plant) factors.

Step 2: Evaluation
External factors include temperature, light, humidity, and wind speed. Plant factors include the number and distribution of stomata, per cent of open stomata, water status of the plant, and canopy structure.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Canopy structure and water status of the plant are plant factors affecting transpiration.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q36 - Tensile strength and capillarity in xylem sap ascent

questiontext.text: The transpiration-driven ascent of xylem sap depends on cohesion, adhesion, and surface tension of water, which together confer high tensile strength and capillarity. In plants, capillarity is aided by:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Capillarity is the ability of a liquid to rise in thin tubes, and it is inversely related to tube diameter.

Step 2: Evaluation
In plants, capillarity is aided by the small diameter of the tracheary elements—specifically the tracheids and vessel elements. Combined with cohesion, adhesion, and surface tension, transpiration can generate forces sufficient to lift a xylem-sized column of water over \(130\text{ metres}\) high.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Capillarity in plants is aided by the small diameter of tracheids and vessel elements.

answer.text: The large diameter of phloem sieve tube elements
The suberised Casparian strips in the leaf epidermis
The small diameter of tracheids and vessel elements

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q37 - Evaporative cooling and purposes of transpiration

questiontext.text: Transpiration serves several important purposes in plants, including cooling leaf surfaces by evaporative cooling up to:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Evaporation of water from leaf surfaces absorbs latent heat, preventing thermal damage under intense sunlight.

Step 2: Evaluation
Transpiration cools leaf surfaces, sometimes by \(10\text{ to }15\) degrees, through evaporative cooling, in addition to creating transpiration pull, supplying water for photosynthesis, transporting minerals, and maintaining cell turgidity.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Evaporative cooling during transpiration can cool leaf surfaces by \(10\text{ to }15\) degrees.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q38 - C4 versus C3 water use efficiency

questiontext.text: Compared to a \(\text{C}_3\) plant, a \(\text{C}_4\) plant is \(\underline{\hspace{2cm}}\) as efficient in fixing carbon dioxide (making sugar), and loses \(\underline{\hspace{2cm}}\) as much water for the same amount of \(\text{CO}_2\) fixed.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The \(\text{C}_4\) photosynthetic pathway evolved as an adaptation to maximise \(\text{CO}_2\) fixation while minimising transpirational water loss.

Step 2: Evaluation
\(\text{C}_4\) plants are twice as efficient as \(\text{C}_3\) plants in terms of fixing carbon dioxide to make sugar. However, for the same amount of \(\text{CO}_2\) fixed, a \(\text{C}_4\) plant loses only half as much water as a \(\text{C}_3\) plant.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A \(\text{C}_4\) plant is twice as efficient in fixing \(\text{CO}_2\) and loses only half as much water.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q39 - Reasons for active absorption of mineral ions

questiontext.text: Why must most mineral nutrients enter plant roots by active absorption rather than solely by passive absorption?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Mineral uptake from soil differs from water uptake due to the ionic nature of minerals and their relative concentrations.

Step 2: Evaluation
Two factors account for active absorption: (1) minerals are present in the soil as charged particles (ions) that cannot move freely across cell membranes, and (2) the concentration of minerals in the soil is usually lower than the concentration of minerals inside the root. Therefore, ATP-dependent active transport is required.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Most minerals require active absorption because they are charged ions and are usually at a lower concentration in the soil than in the root.

answer.text: Minerals are uncharged and their soil concentration is higher than in roots.
Minerals are lipid-soluble and diffuse too rapidly out of root hairs.
Minerals exist as charged ions and their concentration in soil is usually lower than in roots.
Root hairs lack plasma membranes and rely on ATPase pumps in the cell wall.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q40 - Endodermal control points for mineral transport

questiontext.text: What essential role does the root endodermis play in regulating mineral ion transport into the xylem?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Because the Casparian strip blocks apoplastic solute movement, all solutes must pass through endodermal plasma membranes.

Step 2: Evaluation
Transport proteins embedded in the plasma membrane of endodermal cells act as control points where the plant adjusts the quantity and types of solutes reaching the xylem. Furthermore, due to the suberin layer, the root endodermis has the ability to actively transport ions in one direction only.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Endodermal transport proteins act as control points, and the suberin layer enables active transport of ions in one direction only.

answer.text: It allows all soil solutes to enter the xylem non-selectively via apoplast.
It facilitates passive bidirectional leakage of ions from xylem back to cortex.
It converts inorganic mineral ions into sucrose before unloading into xylem.
Its transport proteins act as control points and, due to suberin, it actively transports ions in one direction only.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q41 - Sinks and unloading of mineral ions

questiontext.text: After mineral ions are carried up the stem via the transpiration stream, where and how does their unloading occur?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Mineral ions transported in the xylem are delivered to actively growing and storage regions (sinks).

Step 2: Evaluation
The chief sinks for mineral elements are apical and lateral meristems, young leaves, developing flowers, fruits and seeds, and storage organs. Unloading of mineral ions occurs at the fine vein endings through both diffusion and active uptake by these sink cells.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Unloading occurs at the fine vein endings through diffusion and active uptake by the cells.

answer.text: At the fine vein endings through diffusion and active uptake by sink cells
At the root endodermis exclusively through guttation

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q42 - Remobilisation of mineral elements during senescence

questiontext.text: Before leaf fall in deciduous plants or during senescence of older leaves, which of the following elements is not remobilised to younger parts?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Mineral ions from older, senescing plant parts are frequently withdrawn and exported to younger, growing regions, except for elements bound in permanent structural components.

Step 2: Evaluation
Elements most readily mobilised include phosphorus, sulphur, nitrogen, and potassium. In contrast, elements that are structural components of the cell, such as calcium, are not remobilised.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Calcium is not remobilised from older, senescing leaves.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q43 - Composition of xylem exudates and phloem exchange

questiontext.text: Analysis of xylem exudates reveals that we cannot categorically state that xylem transports only inorganic nutrients while phloem transports only organic materials, because:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Xylem and phloem are not completely isolated in terms of the chemical forms of nutrients they carry.

Step 2: Evaluation
Xylem exudate analysis shows that while some nitrogen travels as inorganic ions, much of it is carried in organic form as amino acids and related compounds. Small amounts of phosphorus and sulphur are also carried as organic compounds, and a small amount of material exchange takes place between xylem and phloem.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Much of the nitrogen in xylem is carried as organic amino acids and related compounds, along with organic forms of P and S and exchange with phloem.

answer.text: Xylem transports sucrose as its primary solute from leaves to roots.
Phloem lacks water and inorganic ions completely.
Much of the nitrogen in xylem travels as organic amino acids, and small amounts of P and S also travel as organic compounds.
Xylem vessels are living cells that synthesise carbohydrates.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q44 - Seasonal reversal of source and sink in phloem

questiontext.text: In early spring, when tree buds require energy for growth and development of the photosynthetic apparatus, how do the roles of roots and buds relate in phloem transport?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In phloem transport, a source is the part that synthesises or mobilises food, and a sink is the part that needs or stores it. This relationship is variable depending on season and plant needs.

Step 2: Evaluation
During early spring, sugar stored in the roots is mobilised so that the roots act as the source, while the developing tree buds act as the sink, resulting in upward translocation in the phloem.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
In early spring, roots act as the source and buds act as the sink.

answer.text: Buds act as the source and roots act as the sink, causing downward phloem flow.
Both roots and buds act as sinks while xylem supplies sucrose.
Phloem transport stops completely until mature leaves develop.
Roots act as the source and buds act as the sink, causing upward phloem flow.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q45 - Composition of phloem sap

questiontext.text: Phloem sap consists mainly of water and sucrose, along with which other substances?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Phloem translocates primarily sucrose from source to sink, but its sap also carries additional organic and signalling compounds.

Step 2: Evaluation
Besides water and sucrose, phloem sap also transports other sugars, hormones, and amino acids.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Phloem sap also transports other sugars, hormones, and amino acids.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q46 - Phloem loading at the source

questiontext.text: According to the pressure flow hypothesis, how does loading of sucrose into phloem sieve tubes at the source initiate mass movement?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Mass flow in phloem is driven by an osmotic pressure gradient established between the source and the sink.

Step 2: Evaluation
At the source, glucose is converted to sucrose, which is actively transported into companion cells and then into living sieve tube cells. This produces a hypertonic condition in the phloem, drawing water from the adjacent xylem by osmosis and increasing hydrostatic pressure to drive sap flow.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Active loading of sucrose creates a hypertonic condition, drawing water from adjacent xylem by osmosis and building hydrostatic pressure.

answer.text: Passive loading creates a hypotonic condition, forcing water out into the xylem.
Active loading creates a hypertonic condition, drawing water from adjacent xylem by osmosis.
Active pumping of water from sink to source creates negative tension in sieve tubes.
Conversion of sucrose to starch inside sieve tubes lowers osmotic pressure.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q47 - Phloem unloading at the sink

questiontext.text: At the sink in the pressure flow hypothesis, what happens after incoming sugars are actively transported out of the phloem?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
To maintain the pressure gradient from source to sink, osmotic pressure at the sink must be reduced.

Step 2: Evaluation
At the sink, sucrose is actively transported out of the phloem into sink cells (where it is used for energy or converted into starch or cellulose). The loss of solute raises the water potential in the phloem, causing water to pass out and eventually return to the xylem.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Loss of solute produces a high water potential in the phloem, and water passes out, returning eventually to the xylem.

answer.text: Water potential in the phloem drops sharply, drawing more water from the xylem.
Osmotic pressure increases, reversing the flow back toward the leaves.
Water potential in the phloem increases, and water passes out, returning to the xylem.
Sieve plates close permanently to prevent water loss.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q48 - Girdling experiment on tree trunk

questiontext.text: In a girdling experiment, a ring of bark up to the depth of the phloem layer is carefully removed from the trunk of a tree. After a few weeks, the bark above the ring becomes swollen because:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Girdling removes the phloem tissue in the bark while leaving the deeper xylem intact.

Step 2: Evaluation
Because the phloem is removed at the ring, downward translocation of food toward the roots is blocked. As a result, organic food accumulates above the ring, causing the portion of the bark above the ring to swell after a few weeks.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The swelling occurs due to the absence of downward movement of food through the phloem.

answer.text: Upward transport of water through the xylem is blocked at the ring.
Roots pump excess mineral ions upward into the bark above the ring.
Guttation occurs through the exposed cambium at the ring.
Downward translocation of food through the phloem is blocked, causing accumulation above the ring.
